title: KAARIGAR Heritage Knowledge Corpus
description: Authoritative curatorial archive of Indian artisanal crafts, master biographies, making stages, and platform policies.

documents.title: KAARIGAR 4-Part Transparent Pricing Formula
documents.content:
KAARIGAR enforces an uncompromised 4-part transparent pricing breakdown on every craftwork:
1. Actual Artisan Price (Base Price): 100% of this amount goes directly to the master craftsperson or guild.
2. Platform Infrastructure Fee: A modest 5% fee dedicated strictly to secure digital archiving, 3D photogrammetry, high-resolution media hosting, and artisan technical onboarding.
3. Applicable Taxes (GST): Exact 5% statutory goods and services tax.
4. Total Final Price: The clear arithmetic sum (Base Price + 5% Platform Fee + 5% Tax). No hidden markups, distributor cuts, or dealer margins.

documents.title: Master-Bench Inspection & Certificate of Authenticity
documents.content: Every single piece catalogued on KAARIGAR undergoes rigorous physical master-bench examination before dispatch. Each certified item arrives with a tamper-evident, serialised Certificate of Authenticity embedded with: (1) The artisan's registered fingerprint or seal, (2) Geographical Indication (GI) registry registration number, (3) Exact material composition breakdown verified by mineral/fibre assay, and (4) An encrypted QR code that leads to the permanent digital ledger entry recording the piece's accession number, lineage, and master maker.

documents.title: Artisan Escrow Protection & 7-Day White-Glove Inspection Window
documents.content: To safeguard both our patrons and our master makers, patron funds are held in secure escrow upon ordering. Artisan payout is released once the piece arrives safely and the patron completes their 7-day white-glove inspection window. All shipments travel in bespoke, climate-cushioned archival crating insured for 100% of value. In the rare circumstance of transit damage, KAARIGAR provides immediate insured recovery and replacement, with zero financial liability on the artisan.

documents.title: Mandatory Authentication for Checkout & Provenance Ownership
documents.content: Patrons must sign in (via mobile OTP or credentials) before completing checkout. This ensures that ownership records, serialised certificates of authenticity, and immutable accession tracking are securely bound to the patron's verified digital profile, preventing unauthorized resale or fraudulent acquisition.

documents.title: Radha & Krishna in the Groves of Kangra (Pahari Miniature)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Radha & Krishna in the Groves of Kangra'.
Craft Tradition: Pahari Miniature Painting (Kangra Kalam revival, circa 1780 Gita Govinda lineage).
Master Artist: Pandit Ram Swaroop Sharma (Chamba-Kangra Parampara Gurukulam, Himachal Pradesh).
Base Price: ₹48,500 INR.
Materials: Handmade Wasli Paper (laminated with rice-starch & neem paste), genuine Badakhshan Lapis Lazuli ultramarine, Deccan Malachite mineral green, Cinnabar vermilion, and 24K beaten gold leaf (varq illumination).
Technique: Painted with a single-hair brush gathered from the throat of a Himalayan mountain squirrel. Agate stone burnishing (ghontai) imparts a cold milk-silk sheen to the paper.
Dimensions: 28.5 cm × 21.0 cm (Framed: 42 cm × 34 cm in teak & glass mount). Weight: 1.4 kg.
Ideal Placements: Curated art wall, reading nook focal point, intimate salon.

documents.title: Cobalt Meena Arabesque Urn (Jaipur Blue Pottery)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Cobalt Meena Arabesque Urn'.
Craft Tradition: Jaipur Blue Pottery (Turko-Persian glazed faience lineage, Sanganer, Rajasthan).
Master Ceramist: Mahesh Kumar & Sanganer Guild (UNESCO Seal of Excellence awardee).
Base Price: ₹24,000 INR.
Materials: 70% Ground Quartz Rock from the Aravalli hills, 15% recycled glass powder, natural Katira Gond, Fuller's earth (Multani Mitti 5%), Cobalt Oxide & Copper Carbonate pigments, low-fire Borax & Feldspar glaze. Completely 100% clay-free.
Technique: Hand-pressed into two-part terracotta open molds with wood ash internal cores, painted freehand with camel-hair brushes, and fired at 850°C in an indigenous wood-fired kiln.
Dimensions: 38.0 cm Height × 22.5 cm Diameter. Weight: 3.6 kg.
Ideal Placements: Entryway console, shelf accent, table centerpiece, mantelpiece.

documents.title: Chanderi Royal Peacock Zari Weave (Handwoven Brocade)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Chanderi Royal Peacock Zari Weave'.
Craft Tradition: Handwoven Chanderi Brocade (Vedic gossamer silk tradition, Pranpur, Madhya Pradesh).
Master Artisan: Master Weaver Bismillah Ansari (Sant Kabir National Awardee · 5th Generation Weaver).
Base Price: ₹36,500 INR.
Materials: Pure un-degummed Mulberry Silk warp (20/22 denier) preserving natural sericin for crystalline drape, fine 120s count cotton weft, real silver electroplated gold zari thread, natural Manjistha (madder root) crimson dye.
Technique: Woven in subterranean earthen pit-looms with foot-treadle tension control. Extra-weft kadwa interlocking ensures each golden peacock motif is an isolated island of zari with no loose floats on the underside.
Dimensions: 5.5 m Length × 1.15 m Width (with blouse piece). Weight: 520 g (ultra-fine gossamer).
Ideal Placements: Draped statement textile, framed fabric panel, formal lounge accent.

documents.title: Bastar Lost-Wax Ritual Guardian Horse (Dhokra Bell Metal)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Bastar Lost-Wax Ritual Guardian Horse'.
Craft Tradition: Bastar Dhokra Lost-Wax Metalcraft (Cire Perdue, 4,000-year Harappan metallurgical lineage).
Master Sculptor: Sukhruram Ghadwa (Ghadwa tribal community, Kondagaon, Bastar, Chhattisgarh).
Base Price: ₹32,000 INR.
Materials: Traditional bell metal bronze alloy (78% copper, 22% tin), forest wild honeycomb beeswax, Sal tree resin (dammar), and riverbed alluvial clay with termite soil.
Technique: Wax is extruded through hardwood presses into gossamer threads and coiled concentric spirals around an inner clay core. Molten bronze at 1200°C vaporizes the wax entirely. The clay mold is broken open with an iron mallet, rendering every casting 100% unique.
Dimensions: 34.0 cm Height × 29.5 cm Length × 12.0 cm Depth. Weight: 4.8 kg.
Ideal Placements: Executive desk accent, coffee table sculptural anchor, bookshelf display, sideboard centerpiece.

documents.title: Temple Spire & Avian Harmony Totem (Channapatna Woodcraft)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Temple Spire & Avian Harmony Totem'.
Craft Tradition: Channapatna Lathe-Turned Woodcraft (Gombegala Ooru / Toy Town, Ramanagara, Karnataka).
Master Craftsman: Syed Khaleel & Sons (Master Wood Turner · 38 Years Atelier Practice).
Base Price: ₹18,500 INR.
Materials: Sustainably harvested Aale Mara / Ivory Wood (Wrightia tinctoria), seasoned Indian Rosewood base, natural Kerria lacca vegetable resin, botanical dyes (turmeric amber, indigo blue, vermilion red).
Technique: Hand-turned on high-speed treadle lathes, vegetable-lac sticks applied through dry friction heat, and buffed with Talegari (palm leaves) to achieve a glass-like child-safe organic luster.
Dimensions: 52.0 cm Height × 15.0 cm Base Diameter. Weight: 2.2 kg.
Ideal Placements: Minimalist corner pedestal, tall bookshelf niche, console sculptural punctuation.

documents.title: Navratna Polki & Enamel Kundan Amulet (Jaipur Royal Court)
documents.content:
Flagship Masterwork: 'Navratna Polki & Enamel Kundan Amulet'.
Craft Tradition: Jaipur Royal Kundan & Meenakari (Mughal-Rajput court goldsmithing lineage, Jaipur, Rajasthan).
Master Goldsmith: Sunar Govind Lal Meenakar (7th Generation Court Goldsmith).
Base Price: ₹89,000 INR.
Materials: 24K refined Kundan gold foil, 22K yellow gold base framework, natural uncut Polki diamonds, Colombian emerald cabochon, and vitreous champlevé mineral enamels (peacock blue, ruby red, bottle green).
Technique: Four-stage classical synthesis: Ghaat (framework shaping), Khudai (intaglio engraving of floral wells), Meenakari (kiln-fired vitreous enamel filling on the reverse), and Jadai (setting uncut gems with cold-burnished 24K pure gold leaf).
Dimensions: 7.8 cm Height × 5.4 cm Width. Weight: 46 g (Net Gold: 34 g 22K/24K).
Ideal Placements: Display vitrine, vanity tray, museum-grade shadowbox frame.

documents.title: Kasuti Embroidery of Karnataka (GI Protected)
documents.content:
Kasuti is an intricate count-thread embroidery tradition native to the Dharwad and North Karnataka region, dating back to the Chalukya era. Craftswomen embroider without knotting the thread or tracing outlines, working stitch-by-stitch counted against the warp and weft of Ilkal handloom sarees.
Four distinct stitches characterize authentic Kasuti:
1. Gavanti (Double running stitch forming straight lines, completely reversible on both sides).
2. Murgi (Zig-zag stepped stitch creating diamond patterns).
3. Neygi (Running stitch resembling woven tapestry).
4. Menthi (Cross-stitch used for dense floral and temple Gopura fills).
Traditional motifs include temple chariots (rathas), tulsi katte, peacocks, elephants, and sacred geometric kolams. Master awardees include Parvati Devi.

documents.title: Bidriware Damascene Metalcraft of Bidar (GI Protected)
documents.content:
Bidriware is an archaic metal handicraft originating from Bidar in northern Karnataka, developed during the 14th-century Bahmani Sultanate. The body is cast from an alloy of zinc (95%) and copper (5%). The surface is engraved with intricate arabesques, and pure silver wire or sheet is hammered into the chiselled grooves (Tarkashi and Tehnishan inlay techniques).
The magic of Bidriware occurs during the final boiling in a paste containing soil gathered exclusively from beneath the foundation of the 500-year-old Bidar Fort, rich in natural potassium nitrate. The paste turns the zinc alloy a deep velvety matte jet-black, leaving the pure silver gleaming with celestial contrast.

documents.title: Mata ni Pachedi (Mother Goddess Shrines of Gujarat)
documents.content:
Mata ni Pachedi ('That which behind the Mother lies') is a sacred ritual textile art practiced by the nomadic Chitara community along the Sabarmati River in Gujarat. Originating when marginalized Vaghari tribes were forbidden from entering stone temples, they painted portable nomadic shrines onto unbleached cotton cloths.
Drawn freehand using bamboo reed pens (kalam) and hand-carved date wood blocks. Dyes are 100% natural: black from fermented iron shavings and jaggery, crimson red from alum mordant boiled with madder root (alizarin), and white reserved un-dyed cloth. Every cloth is consecrated through river washings.

documents.title: Kashmiri Walnut Wood Carving (Juglans Regia)
documents.content:
Kashmiri Walnut Wood Carving is centered in the Kashmir Valley, utilizing exclusively the timber of Juglans regia (indigenous walnut trees) that have reached natural maturity (over 100 years old). The timber is dry-cured for two to three years to eliminate sap moisture and prevent warping.
Master carvers employ four levels of carving: (1) Deep relief (Akkasi), (2) Undercut hollowed carving (Jali work), (3) Shallow engraving, and (4) Semi-relief. Iconic motifs include Chinar leaves, Kashmiri iris, trailing grapevines, and Mughal geometric lattice windows. Finished with natural beeswax and agate burnishing.

documents.title: Patan Patola Double Ikat (Queen of Silks)
documents.content:
Patan Patola from northern Gujarat is the pinnacle of double-ikat weaving worldwide. Both the silk warp and weft threads are individually tied and dyed with natural botanical resists (turmeric, madder, marigold, pomegranate rind) before touching the loom. When woven, the warp and weft meet with mathematical sub-millimeter precision to form identical geometric patterns on both the front and reverse sides of the textile.
A single Patola takes a family of master weavers four to eight months of continuous calculation on a slant-beam rosewood loom. Celebrated in Gujarati lore: 'Padi patole bhat, fatey pan fitey nahin' (The fabric may tear with centuries, but the sacred color shall never fade).

documents.title: The Breath on Wasli: Why Kangra Miniatures Cannot Be Rushed
documents.content:
In Pandit Ram Swaroop Sharma's atelier in the Kangra Valley, time is measured not by clocks but by stone burnishing and pigment settling. Wasli paper requires laminating three sheets of acid-free rag paper with neem-infused starch paste to prevent pest infestation. Once sun-cured against marble slabs, the artist rubs the surface with a heated agate stone until it acquires the dense smoothness of ivory.
Sharma uses a squirrel-hair brush with three hairs plucked from a wild mountain squirrel. As Sharma explains: 'A miniature is meant to be held inches from your eyelashes. If your heartbeat accelerates, the brush wavers. To paint the divine romance, the artist must silence all thoughts of the market. When you grind a mountain stone, light enters the crystal and stays for four hundred years.'

documents.title: The Four-Thousand-Year Wire: Bastar's Lost-Wax Lineage
documents.content:
In the Sal forests of Bastar, metal begins with wild honey hunters who climb trees to harvest combs. Tribal master Sukhruram Ghadwa blends raw beeswax with Sal tree resin (dammar) and strains it into cold river water. The elastic wax is hand-extruded through hardwood presses into gossamer threads, which are wound in concentric spirals over a sun-dried clay core.
Sukhruram reflects: 'There is no master mold. When we pour molten bell metal bronze at twelve hundred degrees, the beeswax vaporizes into smoke. It gives its life so the bronze can take its place. To create one horse, the wax must die.' Because each clay mold is shattered with an iron mallet upon cooling, every single Dhokra sculpture is an irreproducible, singular monument of archaic metallurgy.

documents.title: The Woven Air of the Bundelkhand Plains
documents.content:
Step down into the subterranean pit-loom workshop of Master Weaver Bismillah Ansari in Pranpur, and the intense summer heat drops ten degrees. The packed damp earthen floor preserves the vital moisture of fine 20/22 denier mulberry silk. Ansari's hands dance across the wooden reed with rhythmic percussion as foot treadles control warp tension.
'Chanderi is distinct because of its transparent structure,' Ansari explains. 'We do not boil off the natural sericin gum before weaving, giving the fabric its crystalline transparency and characteristic soft crackle.' Each peacock motif on the pallu is hand-interlocked with the kadwa extra-weft technique, eliminating all loose underside floats. Through KAARIGAR's fair-trade economics, 86% of the purchase price flows directly into the Pranpur weaver collective.

documents.title: Cire Perdue: The Lost-Wax Casting Cycle of Bastar Dhokra
documents.content:
The archaic 5-stage Dhokra manufacturing cycle:
1. Core Sculpting: River alluvial clay mixed with termite hill earth and rice husk forms the inner armature.
2. Wax Thread Coiling: Beeswax and dammar resin are extruded into 1mm threads and coiled over the core.
3. Secondary Moulding: Layers of fine clay slip and coarse sand encase the wax structure with pouring channels.
4. De-waxing & Pouring: The mould is fired in an earthen trench; molten bronze (copper + tin) is poured at 1200°C.
5. Mould Shattering & Patination: After cooling, the outer clay casing is broken open to release the unique bronze piece.

documents.title: Frit, Firing, and Mineral Oxides: The Non-Clay Alchemy of Jaipur Blue Pottery
documents.content:
The 4-stage non-clay dough fabrication of Jaipur Blue Pottery:
1. Dough Compounding: Ground quartz rock (70%), recycled soda glass powder (15%), katira gum, and multani mitti are kneaded into clay-free dough.
2. Mould Casting: Pressed into shallow terracotta open moulds filled with wood ash cores to maintain wall thickness.
3. Mineral Painting: Camel-hair brushes apply cobalt oxide (royal blue) and copper oxide (turquoise) freehand.
4. Borax Glazing & Kiln Firing: Coated with powdered glass, borax, and feldspar glaze, then fired once at 850°C for three days of gradual cooling.
